item.title: "Going to be permanent": Trump on making a deal with Iran
item.description: US President Donald Trump on Saturday said that any potential agreement with Iran would be "permanent" and aimed at preventing Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons, reiterating his insistence on ...
item.content:encoded:
"Going to be permanent": Trump on making a deal with Iran US President Donald Trump on Saturday said that any potential agreement with Iran would be "permanent" and aimed at preventing Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons, reiterating his insistence on securing what he described as a genuine and lasting deal with the country. ANI | Updated: 21-11-2026 22:02 IST | Created: 21-11-2026 22:02 IST

US President Donald Trump (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US President Donald Trump on Saturday said that any potential agreement with Iran would be "permanent" and aimed at preventing Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons, reiterating his insistence on securing what he described as a genuine and lasting deal with the country. "I'm going to make a deal that is going to be permanent. I’m not going to let somebody allow them to have a nuclear weapon," Trump said, expressing his determination to ensure that Iran does not develop nuclear weapons. In an interview with Fox News, Trump also said he had never been particularly interested in regime change in Iran while describing his attacks on the country's senior leadership as a significant shift for the Iranian regime. He characterised Iran's new leadership as "more rational", but questioned its reliability in negotiations, alleging that Tehran had a history of making agreements and subsequently breaking them. The latest remarks come amid continuing tensions between Washington and Tehran, with Trump repeatedly expressing dissatisfaction over the terms Iran has been willing to offer in negotiations. Earlier on Friday, following his visit to China, Trump launched a sharp criticism of Tehran, accusing Iran of misleading people for decades and insisting that any agreement with Washington must meet US expectations. Speaking at a press conference, the US President linked fluctuations in gasoline prices to the outcome of negotiations with Iran, arguing that Tehran wanted an agreement but had not offered terms acceptable to him. "The prices of gasoline now, that also depends on how we settle up with Iran. They want to make a deal, but they don't want to make a deal that's acceptable to me. We want to make a real deal, not a fake deal that they've been doing for 51 years. No longer 47. People talk 47. It's 51 years," Trump said. Taking a further swipe at Tehran, Trump accused Iran of misleading people over the past five decades, remarking, "They've been bullsh***ing people for 51 years." Trump's latest comments underscore his continued push for an agreement that would prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons, while maintaining that Washington would not accept a deal that falls short of its expectations. His remarks come amid continuing tensions in West Asia, with Washington weighing its options regarding Iran, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has reportedly urged the US administration to consider renewed military action against Tehran. While Trump has indicated that he is seeking a lasting diplomatic agreement, his statements also reflect his continued criticism of Iran's negotiating approach and the terms offered by Tehran. (ANI)

item.title: FBI's National Crime database hit by hackers in 2nd breach in recent months
item.description: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is investigating an apparent cyberattack targeting its National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a nationwide database used by law enforcement agencies to ...
item.content:encoded:
FBI's National Crime database hit by hackers in 2nd breach in recent months The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is investigating an apparent cyberattack targeting its National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a nationwide database used by law enforcement agencies to access criminal records, warrants and background-check information, CNN reported, citing two people briefed on the investigation. ANI | Updated: 21-11-2026 21:47 IST | Created: 21-11-2026 21:47 IST

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is investigating an apparent cyberattack targeting its National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a nationwide database used by law enforcement agencies to access criminal records, warrants and background-check information, CNN reported, citing two people briefed on the investigation. According to CNN, the latest intrusion marks the second reported breach involving the FBI in recent months and raises concerns over the security of a critical information-sharing system used by federal, state and local law enforcement agencies across the United States. The NCIC database serves as a key resource for law enforcement authorities nationwide, facilitating the exchange of information on outstanding warrants and background checks. The latest breach was discovered in recent days, according to CNN. The development comes as the Trump administration faces concerns over the country's cybersecurity preparedness following a series of high-profile outages affecting banks, the National Security Agency (NSA) and the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) air traffic control system. Meanwhile, FBI Director Kash Patel appeared on Fox News on Thursday, after bureau officials had learned of the latest cybersecurity incident, to highlight the agency's efforts to strengthen cybersecurity. During the appearance, Patel spoke about Operation Winter Shield, an initiative completed months earlier that sought to encourage companies to update their systems and prevent hackers from accessing sensitive information. Patel also credited the current administration with making upgrades to critical systems aimed at protecting the country's essential infrastructure. "Other administrations could have made these updates, but they didn’t," Patel said. "We are staying ahead of the curve and making up for lost time." Highlighting the potential implications of the latest breach, a former FBI official who had led investigations into cybercriminal groups told CNN that the NCIC database was among the most important information-sharing platforms used by law enforcement agencies. The former FBI official also raised concerns about the possibility of hackers compromising the reliability of information stored in the database, beyond the potential exposure of sensitive records. The latest incident follows another reported cyberattack in September, when a hacking group known as ShinyHunters targeted sensitive personal information belonging to FBI employees through a bureau recruitment website. Earlier, CNN reported that some FBI employees were left uncertain about whether their personal information had been compromised in the incident and expressed dissatisfaction with the security assistance and resources being offered to those affected. A Canadian cybersecurity researcher and author has been arrested and faces charges in connection with the ShinyHunters breach. The FBI had also experienced an earlier cyber incident in 2023, when hackers accessed a computer system used by its New York field office for investigations into child sexual exploitation. According to CNN's report, the compromised system included one used to store images related to the Jeffrey Epstein investigation. (ANI)

item.title: 5.7-magnitude earthquake strikes China
item.description: An earthquake of magnitude 5.7 struck China at a depth of 80 kilometres on Saturday, the National Center for Seismology (NCS) said, reporting another seismic event in the country earlier this month.
item.content:encoded:
5.7-magnitude earthquake strikes China An earthquake of magnitude 5.7 struck China at a depth of 80 kilometres on Saturday, the National Center for Seismology (NCS) said, reporting another seismic event in the country earlier this month. ANI | Updated: 21-11-2026 17:18 IST | Created: 21-11-2026 17:18 IST

Representational Image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

An earthquake of magnitude 5.7 struck China at a depth of 80 kilometres on Saturday, the National Center for Seismology (NCS) said, reporting another seismic event in the country earlier this month. According to the NCS, the earthquake occurred at 4:15:37 pm IST on November 21, at latitude 37.099° North and longitude 96.482° East, with its location reported in China. In a post on X, the National Center for Seismology stated, "EQ of M: 5.7, On: 21/11/2026 16:15:37 IST, Lat: 37.099 N, Long: 96.482 E, Depth: 80 Km, Location: China." The latest earthquake comes after a 4.4-magnitude tremor was recorded in China on November 5. The earlier earthquake occurred at 6:19:17 am IST at a shallow depth of 10 kilometres, with its epicentre at latitude 32.592° North and longitude 94.291° East, according to the NCS. In its post on X, the NCS reported, "EQ of M: 4.4, On: 05/11/2026 06:19:17 IST, Lat: 32.592 N, Long: 94.291 E, Depth: 10 Km, Location: China." The two earthquakes fall into different depth categories under the classification outlined by the United States Geological Survey (USGS). While the November 5 earthquake, at a depth of 10 kilometres, falls in the shallow category, the latest tremor, recorded at 80 kilometres, is classified as an intermediate-depth earthquake. According to the USGS, earthquakes occurring between 0 and 70 kilometres are classified as shallow, those between 70 and 300 kilometres as intermediate, and those between 300 and 700 kilometres as deep earthquakes. The USGS further explains that the term "deep-focus earthquakes" is generally applied to earthquakes occurring at depths greater than 70 kilometres. It also notes that all earthquakes deeper than 70 kilometres are localised within great slabs of lithosphere that are sinking into the Earth's mantle. Explaining the relationship between earthquake depth and surface shaking, the USGS states that "the strength of shaking from an earthquake diminishes with increasing distance from the earthquake's source". It further observes that shaking at the surface from an earthquake occurring at 500 kilometres deep is considerably less than that from an earthquake of the same magnitude occurring at 20 kilometres depth. The USGS also states that earthquakes occur in the crust or upper mantle, which extends from the Earth's surface to about 800 kilometres. (ANI)
